plan.topic: Plague 101: how one bacterium (Yersinia pestis) causes three different forms of disease (bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic), how each starts, what it does in the body, and why only pneumonic can pass between people
plan.angle:
An evergreen explainer that rests only on CDC and WHO pages: About Plague (updated Aug 24, 2026), How Plague Spreads, Signs and Symptoms of Plague (use that exact title) and the WHO plague fact sheet, each cited by its exact title and updated date.

News context: one neutral sentence at most ('plague has been in the news this month'). Say nothing about the Irkutsk case's status, tests, quarantine or WHO/Russian statements.

Segments:
(1) The bacterium and its natural cycle: wild rodents and their fleas (CDC).
(2) Bubonic: a flea bite or handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal; the bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells (CDC wording).
(3) Septicemic: infection in the bloodstream. It can be the first form, or it can follow untreated bubonic plague (CDC).
(4) Pneumonic: infection in the lungs. It can start by breathing in infectious droplets, or follow untreated bubonic or septicemic plague. Use CDC's exact lines: 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people' and 'Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague'. Sick cats are CDC's example.
(5) Why the form changes the public-health response: why contacts of pneumonic cases are traced, and why bubonic cases aren't. Keep this general, with no Irkutsk details.
(6) Symptoms of each form, taken from Signs and Symptoms of Plague. List CDC's 4 pneumonic signs in full: fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain. Give no incubation numbers unless they're copied verbatim from the CDC page; incubation is S1's topic.
(7) Treatment: 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early' (CDC/WHO). No drug names, doses, stockpiling or self-treatment.
(8) Calm fact in CDC's wording: 'Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.'

Scope discipline: never widen a pneumonic-only claim to all plague. Credit a line to a source only if that page says it word for word, or as a close paraphrase without quote marks.

Close: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Then 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'

Visuals: labelled diagrams of lymph nodes, blood and lungs. No clinical photos, no rats as horror, no skulls.

Description: plain text, 1,500 characters or fewer, up to 4 CDC/WHO sources with their updated dates.
plan.working_title: Plague: Bubonic vs Pneumonic vs Septicemic, How One Bacterium Causes 3 Diseases
plan.why: Every news explainer contrasts the plague forms, and the analytics single this topic out as one that failed only because of the carousel format. It rests fully on settled CDC and WHO pages, with no case-status claims to date or attribute, so it should pass the fact-check on the first try.

package.description:
Quick answer: CDC says pneumonic plague (lungs) is the only form that can spread from person to person, through infectious droplets, typically with direct and close contact. Bubonic (lymph node) and septicemic (bloodstream) plague usually come from a flea bite or handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal; WHO describes human-to-human spread of bubonic plague as rare. Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early.

Plague has been in the news this month; this video covers settled CDC and WHO science, not any current case.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. After a possible exposure, if you develop symptoms, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
CDC, About Plague (updated Aug 24, 2026): https://www.cdc.gov/plague/about/index.html
CDC, How Plague Spreads (updated May 15, 2024): https://www.cdc.gov/plague/causes/index.html
CDC, Signs and Symptoms of Plague (updated May 15, 2024): https://www.cdc.gov/plague/signs-symptoms/index.html
WHO, Plague fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague

script.working_title: Pneumonic vs Bubonic Plague (and Septicemic): How One Bacterium Causes 3 Diseases
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim + open loop: one bacterium causes three different diseases, CDC says only one spreads between people, and a century-old CDC date is promised in the first 30 seconds and paid off near the end

scenes.narration: One bacterium. Three very different diseases. And according to CDC, only one of them can spread from person to person.

visual.stock_query: one bacterium splitting into three paths

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: counterintuitive claim in the first 5 seconds

scenes.narration: The germ is the same every time. What changes is the doorway it uses to get in, and where in your body it settles.
scenes.retention_device: Curiosity gap: what are the three doorways?

scenes.narration: Plague has been in the news this month, so let's get the basics right, using only what CDC and the World Health Organization actually say.

visual.stock_query: friendly narrator holding CDC WHO pages

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll learn how each form starts, what it does inside the body, and the symptoms CDC lists for each one.
scenes.on_screen_text: How it starts. What it does.

items: What it does in the body

scenes.retention_device: Promise: clear roadmap of the payoff

scenes.narration: And stay to the end, because one sentence on a CDC page puts person-to-person spread in the United States into perspective. It's a date. And it's more than a century old.

visual.stock_query: old calendar page with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop: the century-old CDC date, paid off in 'The 1924 fact'

scenes.narration: First, meet the germ.
Plague is caused by a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. CDC describes plague as a disease that affects humans and other mammals.
Its natural home isn't people. WHO says it's usually found in small mammals and their fleas, and it's passed between animals through fleas.

visual.stock_query: cute small mammals with tiny fleas

scenes.retention_device: Reframe: plague is mainly an animal disease

scenes.narration: Picture a quiet loop running in the wild. Rodent to flea, flea to rodent, mostly out of sight.
So how do people get pulled in? CDC says humans usually get plague after being bitten by a rodent flea carrying the bacterium, or by handling an animal infected with plague.

items: Bite from an infected rodent flea

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, answered immediately

scenes.narration: And timing matters. CDC explains that during plague outbreaks among animals, many rodents die, and hungry fleas go looking for other sources of blood.

visual.stock_query: cartoon flea searching with magnifying glass

scenes.narration: CDC says people and animals visiting places where rodents have recently died from plague are at risk. Dogs and cats can also bring infected fleas into the home.

visual.stock_query: dog and cat walking into house

scenes.narration: Plague still occurs naturally today. WHO says that during 2019 to 2025, most cases reported to WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising fact: plague is still around

scenes.narration: So why does one germ cause three different illnesses? It comes down to where it lands first. Let's start with the most common form.
Bubonic plague is the form most people picture, and WHO calls it the most common form of plague.
It usually starts with a flea bite. But CDC says it can also follow handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal.

items: Handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal

scenes.narration: CDC's example is a hunter skinning a rabbit or other infected animal without using proper precautions.
Then the bacteria do something sneaky. They don't stay at the bite. WHO says they travel through the lymphatic system, part of your immune defences.
Their destination is a lymph node, one of the small filters along that network. CDC says the bacteria multiply in a lymph node near where they entered the body.
That node becomes swollen and painful. CDC calls these swollen nodes buboes, and that's where bubonic plague gets its name.

visual.stock_query: cartoon lymph node swelling labelled bubo

scenes.narration: Here's the detail to hold onto. CDC says if the patient isn't treated with the appropriate antibiotics, the bacteria can spread to other parts of the body.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop: where does it spread next?

scenes.narration: Where they spread decides what happens next. And that brings us to form number two.

visual.stock_query: arrow from lymph node to blood

scenes.narration: Septicemic plague is infection in the bloodstream.
Instead of being held at one lymph node, the bacteria are multiplying in the blood itself.
CDC says there are two routes here. Septicemic plague can occur as the first symptom of plague, or it can develop from untreated bubonic plague.

items: As the first form of plague

scenes.narration: And it can begin the same ways bubonic plague does. CDC's page on how plague spreads says flea bites, and handling an infected animal's tissue or fluids, can lead to either bubonic or septicemic plague.
Here's the tricky part. CDC's symptom list for septicemic plague doesn't include the swollen lymph node. So one of plague's most recognisable clues may be missing.
scenes.on_screen_text: The swollen node may be missing

scenes.narration: Notice what's missing so far: spread between people. According to CDC, that only enters the picture when the bacteria reach the lungs.
Pneumonic plague is infection in the lungs. CDC calls it the most serious form of the disease.
It can start in two ways. CDC says it can develop from breathing in infectious droplets, or from untreated bubonic or septicemic plague after the bacteria spread to the lungs.

items: From untreated bubonic or septicemic plague

scenes.narration: Remember that detail from bubonic plague? This is where it can lead. Left untreated, the infection can spread and reach the lungs.

visual.stock_query: path from lymph node to lungs

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the bubonic open loop

scenes.narration: Once it's in the lungs, the bacteria have a new exit. CDC explains that a person with plague pneumonia may cough droplets containing the bacteria into the air.
If another person breathes those droplets in, CDC says they can develop pneumonic plague.
And here's the line that matters most. In CDC's words: Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.

visual.quote: Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.

scenes.narration: So among the three forms, CDC says pneumonic plague is the only one that can be spread from person to person.
But how close do you have to be? CDC answers that too.
Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.

visual.quote: Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.

scenes.narration: Direct and close contact. Hold onto that phrase, because it shapes how health agencies respond.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop: how agencies use it

scenes.narration: And did you catch the word animal? Here's where it gets surprising.
CDC's example isn't a rat. It's a sick cat.
CDC says sick cats can pass infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians. So the close-contact rule applies to animals with pneumonic plague too.
Now, why does any of this matter beyond biology? Because the form decides who public-health teams need to find.
With bubonic or septicemic plague, the usual source is a flea or an infected animal, not another person. WHO describes human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague as rare.
So the usual question is where the person was exposed: the fleas, the animals, the place.
That fits what CDC says: not every form of plague passes from one person to another. CDC says only pneumonic plague can, and WHO calls person-to-person spread of bubonic plague rare.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not every form spreads person to person

visual.myth: Every form of plague spreads person to person
visual.fact: CDC: only pneumonic plague can spread person to person. WHO: bubonic person-to-person spread is rare

scenes.narration: With pneumonic plague, the picture changes. Now the people who were in direct and close contact with the patient matter.

visual.stock_query: circle of contacts around patient icon

scenes.narration: WHO's outbreak guidance includes isolating patients with pneumonic plague, and identifying and monitoring their close contacts.

WHO says close contacts of pneumonic plague patients, and household members of bubonic plague patients, should be given preventive antibiotics. That's a decision for clinicians and public-health teams, never something to do on your own.
scenes.retention_device: Safety caveat tied to the action

scenes.narration: It's that CDC sentence in action. If spread typically requires direct and close contact, finding those close contacts is how you break the chain.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'hold onto that phrase' loop

scenes.narration: But tracing only works if someone recognises the illness first. So what does each form actually look like?

visual.stock_query: question mark over three body diagrams

scenes.narration: Signs and symptoms. Everything here comes from CDC's page, Signs and Symptoms of Plague.
First, the overlap. Fever and weakness appear on CDC's list for all three forms.
For bubonic plague, CDC lists fever, headache, chills, weakness, and one or more swollen and painful lymph nodes, called buboes.
scenes.retention_device: List card: new visual every few seconds

scenes.narration: For septicemic plague: fever and chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock, and possibly bleeding into the skin and other organs.

items: Possibly bleeding into skin and other organs

scenes.narration: CDC adds that skin and other tissues may turn black and die, especially on the fingers, toes and nose. It shows how serious a bloodstream infection can become.
For pneumonic plague: fever, headache, weakness, and a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucus.

items: Rapidly developing pneumonia: shortness of breath, chest pain, cough

scenes.narration: If you remember just four signs for pneumonic plague, make them these: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain.
These signs aren't unique to plague. WHO lists bubonic plague symptoms as sudden fever, chills, head and body aches, weakness, vomiting and nausea, and those can come with many other illnesses too.

visual.stock_query: puzzled doctor with many illness cards

scenes.narration: That's why context matters: where you've been, and what you or your pets may have been exposed to.

visual.stock_query: map pin hiking trail and pet

scenes.narration: And context leads to the most hopeful part of this story.
Let's be honest about the stakes first.

visual.stock_query: chapter card clock and pill bottle

scenes.narration: WHO breaks the risk down by form. Left untreated, bubonic plague kills 30% to 60% of people.

visual.stock_query: big number card lymph node icon

scenes.narration: And untreated pneumonic and septicaemic plague? WHO says they are always fatal.

visual.stock_query: big text card lungs blood icons

scenes.narration: Now the flip side. Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early. That's the message from both CDC and WHO.
For pneumonic plague specifically, WHO says recovery rates are high if it's detected and treated in time, within 24 hours of symptoms starting.

visual.stat_label: Pneumonic: treated in time, recovery high (WHO)

scenes.narration: Same bacterium, very different outcome. The difference is time.
So if you've heard that plague has no cure, that's not what the health agencies say.
scenes.on_screen_text: No cure? Not per CDC, WHO

visual.fact: Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC, WHO)

scenes.retention_device: Myth correction of a circulating belief

scenes.narration: One important line, though. Which antibiotic, and how much, is a decision for a doctor. Don't self-treat or stockpile; prompt medical care is what works.
Which brings us back to that date I promised at the start.
scenes.retention_device: Return to the main open loop

scenes.narration: Plague's reputation is enormous. CDC notes it's infamous for killing millions of people in Europe during the Middle Ages.
So you might expect person-to-person spread to be a regular event. Here's what CDC actually says.
In CDC's words: Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924, but there continue to be rare cases of pneumonic plague among people exposed to sick cats.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not documented in US since 1924 (rare cases from sick cats)

visual.quote: Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924, but there continue to be rare cases of pneumonic plague among people exposed to sick cats.

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: 1924. More than a century without documented person-to-person spread in the US, according to CDC, even though rare pneumonic cases still happen in people exposed to sick cats.

visual.stat_label: US person-to-person spread not documented since (CDC)

scenes.narration: That calm fact fits everything we've covered. According to CDC, spread between people requires the pneumonic form, typically with direct and close contact. And plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early.
Let's lock it in.

One bacterium: Yersinia pestis. Bubonic plague settles in a lymph node near where it entered. Septicemic is in the bloodstream. Pneumonic is in the lungs, and according to CDC, it's the only form that can spread from person to person.

items: Pneumonic: lungs, the only form that spreads person to person (CDC)
visual.stock_query: labelled lymph node blood lungs diagram

scenes.narration: CDC says spread between people happens through infectious droplets, and typically requires direct and close contact with a person or animal with pneumonic plague.

Now, the part to remember. A possible exposure could be a flea bite in an area where plague occurs, handling tissue or body fluids of an animal that may be infected, or close contact with a person or animal with pneumonic plague.

items: Handling tissue or body fluids of a possibly infected animal
Close contact with a person or animal with pneumonic plague

scenes.narration: If that's you, and you develop fever, chills, weakness, a swollen and painful lymph node, or a cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
scenes.on_screen_text: CONTACT A DOCTOR OR LOCAL HEALTH AUTHORITY URGENTLY
scenes.retention_device: Clear call to action for safety

scenes.narration: Don't wait to see if it passes, and don't treat yourself. Getting antibiotics from a doctor early is what makes the difference.
If you're worried, talk to a health professional.
scenes.on_screen_text: If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

factcheck.summary: I checked every factual claim against all four cited pages, fetched on 2026-10-10, and the script is accurate and safe. The verbatim CDC quotes in s34, s37 and s71 match "How Plague Spreads" word for word: the droplets sentence ending "the only way that plague can spread between people", "Typically, this requires direct and close contact…", and the 1924 sentence including the sick-cats clause. The symptom lists in s53, s54 and s56, the septicemic routes, the two ways pneumonic plague starts, and "most serious form" / "only form… spread from person to person" all match "Signs and Symptoms of Plague". The Yersinia pestis line, "humans and other mammals", the flea bite or infected animal routes, the Middle Ages line and "cured with antibiotics… given promptly" all match "About Plague". The WHO lines also match the WHO fact sheet: small mammals and fleas, spread between animals through fleas, the lymphatic system, bubonic as the most common form, human-to-human spread of bubonic plague as rare, the 30–60% figure, "always fatal" for pneumonic and septicaemic plague left untreated, high recovery within 24 hours, most 2019–2025 cases in DRC and Madagascar, isolating patients, identifying and monitoring contacts, and preventive antibiotics for contacts and for household members of bubonic patients. Source years are correct: CDC Spread and Symptoms were last updated May 15, 2024, CDC About on Aug 24, 2026, and the WHO fact sheet on Sep 29, 2026. Safety is good. The video makes no claim about the current case beyond one neutral context sentence, includes no dosing, carries clear no-self-treatment and no-stockpiling caveats, lists all 4 of CDC's pneumonic signs, uses the exact line "contact a doctor or local health authority urgently", and includes "If you're worried, talk to a health professional." The hook pays off: the 1924 date is promised in s05 and delivered in s71–s72. There are 4 small wording issues, each with an exact fix below. None would mislead a viewer.

issues.claim: WHO breaks the risk down by form. Left untreated, bubonic plague kills 30% to 60% of people.
issues.problem: WHO's wording is 'a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 60% for the bubonic type', in a sentence where 'when left untreated' is attached to the pneumonic and septicaemic clause. 'Kills 30% to 60% of people' turns a case-fatality ratio into a general statement, and the 'left untreated' scope is ours rather than clearly WHO's.
issues.fix: Narration: "WHO breaks the risk down by form. For bubonic plague, WHO gives a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 60%." On-screen text: "Bubonic: 30% to 60% case fatality (WHO)". stat_label: "Bubonic plague case-fatality ratio (WHO)"

issues.claim: CDC explains that a person with plague pneumonia may cough droplets containing the bacteria into the air.
issues.problem: CDC says 'Humans and animals with plague pneumonia can sometimes cough droplets…'. The script drops 'sometimes' and the animal half, which s39–s41 rely on.
issues.fix: "Once it's in the lungs, the bacteria have a new exit. CDC explains that people and animals with plague pneumonia can sometimes cough droplets containing the bacteria into the air."

issues.claim: CDC says sick cats can pass infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians.
issues.problem: CDC's actual wording is 'Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians'. The script should use the source's own verb.
issues.fix: "CDC says cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians. So the close-contact rule applies to animals with pneumonic plague too."

issues.problem: The spelling is inconsistent: 'septicaemic' here, but 'Septicemic' in the chapter card and everywhere else. Captions built from this will look mismatched.
issues.fix: Narration: "And untreated pneumonic and septicemic plague? WHO says they are always fatal." On-screen: "Untreated pneumonic, septicemic: always fatal (WHO)". stat_label: "Untreated pneumonic and septicemic plague (WHO)"

audio.soundNotes: Music already sits well inside the target window (-13.5 dB under voice, -13.6 dB in pauses), so gain stays at 1.0; don't push it louder. The main fix is a cluster of ~17 SFX cues (bubbles/blips/pops/swooshes) that measured 4–14 dB louder than the -14 to -20 dB speech target, which would have poked through the narration — these are pulled down or near-killed. Everything else, including the many "swell" cues that read as near-silent, is left alone since it's already under the voice or correctly loud only in true pauses/transitions (-6 to -12 dB). Added five bespoke story-moment SFX (paw/collar, heartbeat, clock ticks, phone chime, bell toll) at low gain to add texture at key reveals without ever competing with the narrator.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with large bold sans-serif headlines and ≤3 short lines of text; no cut-off or overlapping issues. Candidate #0 best matches the exact title ("Pneumonic vs Bubonic... Which One Spreads") with a direct versus layout, two labelled characters, and color-coded X/check icons that create a quick visual puzzle (which one spreads?) without fully spelling out the mechanism — strong contrast (magenta vs blue on purple) and a clear single focal point (the VS). Candidate #1 ("3 FORMS") is a plague-101 generic thumbnail that doesn't pay off this specific title's two-way comparison and has a cheerful, non-tense bacterium mascot, weakening emotional pull for this topic. Candidate #2 ("IT'S THE LUNGS") is clean and legible but answers a slightly different question than the title promises and gives away the payoff immediately with less compositional tension. None are misleading or sensational beyond the title. #0 is the strongest CTR pick while maintaining legibility ≥7.
